name: Confirmation bias
definition: A tendency to attend to or prefer information that supports an existing belief or desired conclusion.
mechanism: Greene describes self-comforting interpretation and selective evidence seeking as a pathway to distorted judgments.
observableIndicators: Looking only for support of a favored plan
Discounting counterarguments without examining them
alternativeExplanations: Time constraints or limited access to contrary evidence can also produce one-sided research
commonMisinterpretations: One mistaken decision does not establish a stable personality trait

name: Emotional reactivity
definition: A change in judgment or behavior associated with heightened emotional arousal, as described in Greene’s chapter.
mechanism: The chapter proposes that intense feelings can narrow attention and encourage rapid reactions.
observableIndicators: Urgent decisions made during interpersonal conflict
alternativeExplanations: Stressors, legitimate danger, and limited information may influence quick action
commonMisinterpretations: The presence of emotion does not make every decision unsound

name: Empathic perspective taking
definition: An effort to understand another person’s situation and point of view without assuming certainty about their thoughts.
mechanism: Greene proposes directed attention, active listening, and revising early impressions.
observableIndicators: Asking clarifying questions
Withholding snap judgments
alternativeExplanations: Perspective taking may be limited by incomplete knowledge or context
commonMisinterpretations: Feeling convinced you know another person’s intentions is not proof of empathy

name: Self-protective rationalization
definition: Post-hoc explanations that favor a flattering account of why a choice was made.
mechanism: Greene associates ego protection with explanations that overlook one’s own contribution to mistakes.
observableIndicators: Assigning all blame to circumstances without examining personal choices
alternativeExplanations: Real structural constraints or incomplete information
commonMisinterpretations: An explanation is not false merely because it protects self-image

name: Analytic empathy
definition: Building a tentative picture of another person’s viewpoint from conversation, context and feedback.
mechanism: Greene recommends combining perspective-taking with direct and indirect correction rather than assuming a first reading is accurate.
observableIndicators: Asking open questions; revising an impression after hearing context
alternativeExplanations: Courtesy or professional requirements can prompt similar listening
commonMisinterpretations: Analytic empathy is not a license to infer private trauma

name: Self-image regulation
definition: The maintenance of a working sense of self-worth in response to attention, comparison and criticism.
mechanism: Greene proposes that a resilient self-concept allows more attention to be directed outward.
observableIndicators: Accepting correction without dramatic retaliation
alternativeExplanations: External safety, resources and power can change reactions
commonMisinterpretations: This is not a verified diagnostic spectrum

name: Impression management
definition: Adjusting public expression to satisfy context-dependent expectations.
mechanism: Greene distinguishes strategic public roles from the private mix of motives and feelings.
observableIndicators: A presenter adopts formal language despite feeling nervous
alternativeExplanations: Cultural courtesy, professional norms and genuine enthusiasm
commonMisinterpretations: A social mask does not automatically mean fraud

name: Nonverbal ambiguity
definition: The fact that gestures, expression and posture may support several explanations.
mechanism: Greene recommends observation in context; inference remains fallible and can be checked through conversation.
observableIndicators: Interpreting hesitant speech only after asking about setting and expectations
alternativeExplanations: Physical condition, cultural habit, fatigue or sensory difference
commonMisinterpretations: A single gesture cannot establish a hidden motive

name: Role-dependent behavior
definition: The variation of expression across social settings and responsibilities.
mechanism: Different audiences, power hierarchies, and roles change what people feel free to say or show.
observableIndicators: Someone behaves more cautiously with a supervisor than with peers
alternativeExplanations: Safety, incentives, and explicit organizational policies
commonMisinterpretations: Different presentation is not proof of an unstable identity

name: Recurring behavioral patterns
definition: Repeated observable choices in comparable situations over time.
mechanism: Greene treats repetition across projects and relationships as a clue to enduring coping tendencies.
observableIndicators: An executive repeatedly retracts delegated authority despite prior promises
alternativeExplanations: Similar external pressures or institutional systems
commonMisinterpretations: History is not destiny; context matters

name: Trait-versus-situation distinction
definition: The difference between an enduring disposition and conduct prompted by immediate conditions.
mechanism: This editorial distinction guards against over-attributing every act to character.
observableIndicators: Comparing reliable performance across equivalent roles and pressure levels
alternativeExplanations: A shortage, safety issue or temporary illness
commonMisinterpretations: One bad deadline is not sufficient evidence of character

name: Behavioral reliability
definition: A practical pattern of following through on commitments and repairing errors.
mechanism: Greene privileges repeatable actions over charisma or public reputation.
observableIndicators: Documented delivery, accountability and adjustment following feedback
alternativeExplanations: Good systems and adequate staffing can support reliability
commonMisinterpretations: Quiet manner is not inherently more virtuous than energetic presentation

name: Projected desire
definition: Anticipated possession can be valued because of the identity, freedom or distinction imagined around an object.
mechanism: The object functions as a carrier for imagined rewards, beyond its use-value.
observableIndicators: Attention intensifies around an unfamiliar object and may recede after acquisition.
alternativeExplanations: Practical quality and affordability can explain interest without projection.
commonMisinterpretations: An intense desire is not necessarily proof of a hidden unmet emotional need.

name: Practical need
definition: A requirement whose absence imposes a material or functional cost, even if there is no socially attractive story around it.
mechanism: Actual function and circumstance, not imagined status, help determine necessity.
observableIndicators: A basic garment meets a requirement even when no one covets its style.
alternativeExplanations: People may legitimately have symbolic and social needs, blurring the boundary.
commonMisinterpretations: A need cannot always be reduced to mere survival.

name: Perceived scarcity and social proof
definition: Limited access or others’ apparent interest may alter anticipated value.
mechanism: Exclusivity and comparison change what the observer believes an object signifies.
observableIndicators: A product receives attention after admired peers discuss it.
alternativeExplanations: Scarcity can also be a sign of poor service or manufactured pressure.
commonMisinterpretations: Limited supply is not evidence of quality or consent.

name: Decision horizon
definition: The interval over which a decision-maker considers outcomes, costs and options.
mechanism: Extending the frame reveals delayed effects and reversibility.
observableIndicators: A plan includes present costs and multi-year maintenance.
alternativeExplanations: A short horizon can be warranted under immediate constraints.
commonMisinterpretations: A long horizon cannot predict surprises with certainty.

name: Salience of immediate rewards
definition: Vivid short-term outcomes can dominate attention at the expense of harder-to-see future costs.
mechanism: Current signals crowd out slower-moving risk information.
observableIndicators: People treat rapid price appreciation as proof of safety.
alternativeExplanations: Current information may be genuinely useful and time critical.
commonMisinterpretations: Reacting quickly is not always irrational.

name: Counterfactual scenario planning
definition: Explicitly considering alternative outcomes and assumptions before acting.
mechanism: Parallel scenarios reduce reliance on a single desired future story.
observableIndicators: A group evaluates success, failure and renegotiation options.
alternativeExplanations: Forecasts can themselves be overconfident or politically biased.
commonMisinterpretations: Scenario planning is not a guarantee against loss.

name: Self-opinion and identity threat
definition: Perceived challenges to competence, goodness or independence can change how a proposal is heard.
mechanism: Social threat competes with evaluating the proposition on its merits.
observableIndicators: A public criticism produces a status-oriented defense.
alternativeExplanations: A person may reject an idea because its consequences are harmful.
commonMisinterpretations: Disagreement is not proof of insecurity.

name: Autonomy-supportive persuasion
definition: An attempt to influence through transparent reasons and genuine capacity to decline.
mechanism: Respect, accessible evidence and voluntary choice can enable reconsideration.
observableIndicators: A manager offers an honest pilot with opt-out and feedback.
alternativeExplanations: Participants may still reject the proposal on its merits.
commonMisinterpretations: Appearing respectful without allowing refusal is not sufficient.

name: Coercive pressure
definition: Influence that relies on threats, material leverage or unreasonable penalties for refusal.
mechanism: Constrained alternatives make compliance a poor proxy for agreement.
observableIndicators: A worker signs because a manager threatens retaliation.
alternativeExplanations: A lawful negotiation can include real costs without automatically being coercion.
commonMisinterpretations: Visible compliance is not evidence of consent.

name: Expectation-behavior feedback
definition: Anticipations affect responses, which can shape others’ responses and appear to confirm initial beliefs.
mechanism: Interpretation and interaction may recursively reinforce one another.
observableIndicators: Guarded speech prompts distance that is read as rejection.
alternativeExplanations: The other party may be hostile regardless of one’s expectations.
commonMisinterpretations: This mechanism does not establish fault for mistreatment.

name: Interpretive attitude
definition: A recurring orientation that shapes attention and meaning assigned to ambiguous events.
mechanism: Predictions influence which cues are noticed and which actions seem possible.
observableIndicators: Two people interpret an uncertain comment differently.
alternativeExplanations: Experience and environment can justify cautious interpretations.
commonMisinterpretations: Positive interpretation should not deny observable harm.

name: External circumstance
definition: Material conditions, institutional rules and actions by others that shape what can happen independently of personal interpretation.
mechanism: Constraints delimit which choices are feasible, regardless of mindset.
observableIndicators: Unaffordable transportation restricts employment options despite motivation.
alternativeExplanations: Some constraints can change through collective action or adaptation.
commonMisinterpretations: Structural conditions should not be used to deny every possibility of agency.

name: Disowned self-image
definition: Parts of behavior or aspiration a person finds difficult to incorporate into their preferred identity.
mechanism: Greene draws on Jungian theory to explain perceived discrepancies between a public persona and admitted impulses.
observableIndicators: Repeatedly denying an observable mistake despite contradictory records.
alternativeExplanations: Role demands, embarrassment, impression management or memory uncertainty.
commonMisinterpretations: A disowned self-image cannot be detected reliably from one inconsistency.

name: Contradictory behavior
definition: A mismatch between stated values, stable self-descriptions, or different observable actions.
mechanism: Inconsistency may indicate competing goals, shifting contexts or an incomplete self-description; it does not specify a unique unconscious mechanism.
observableIndicators: A leader praises candid feedback but excludes critical voices.
alternativeExplanations: Different context, incomplete information, multiple incentives or unfair institutional rules.
commonMisinterpretations: A contradiction proves what a person unconsciously wants.

name: Integration of traits
definition: The reflective acknowledgment of mixed motives and personal capacities without treating every impulse as justified conduct.
mechanism: Greene recommends conscious examination of disowned attitudes and a more flexible self-concept.
observableIndicators: Admitting anger while choosing a constructive response and accepting accountability.
alternativeExplanations: Ordinary reflective learning without a psychodynamic Shadow model.
commonMisinterpretations: Integrating aggression means behaving aggressively.

name: Envy and comparison
definition: Distress or longing in response to another person possessing an advantage judged personally significant.
mechanism: Comparison can affect self-evaluation and attention, but does not by itself determine hostility or sabotage.
observableIndicators: A person acknowledges disappointment when a peer receives an award.
alternativeExplanations: Admiration, disappointment about procedure, jealousy, structural inequity.
commonMisinterpretations: Criticism or silence necessarily means someone is envious.

name: Jealousy and relationship threat
definition: Concern about losing a valued relationship or bond, especially to a perceived rival.
mechanism: Perceived relational competition may elicit vigilance or distress distinct from wanting another’s advantage.
observableIndicators: A partner expresses concern about shifting relationship boundaries.
alternativeExplanations: Insecurity, ordinary renegotiation, concrete betrayal or unmet expectations.
commonMisinterpretations: Jealousy and envy are interchangeable.

name: Admiration versus resentment
definition: Different responses to upward comparison: aspirational respect or negative response to an advantage or suspected injustice.
mechanism: Evaluation of attainability, fairness and personal meaning can change the emotional meaning of a comparison.
observableIndicators: A student studies a peer’s successful method rather than attacking their character.
alternativeExplanations: Genuine procedural complaints, professional disagreement, competitiveness.
commonMisinterpretations: Admiration implies inferiority or resentment always proves envy.

name: Confidence versus overconfidence
definition: Confidence is a level of belief in ability; overconfidence is unwarranted belief when compared with justified accuracy or reliable benchmarks.
mechanism: Calibration requires comparing predictions and claims to evidence in comparable conditions.
observableIndicators: A leader predicts results and revises estimates after new data.
alternativeExplanations: Uncertain environment, asymmetric incentives or an ambitious but calibrated strategy.
commonMisinterpretations: Bold decision-making alone proves irrational grandiosity.

name: Success attribution
definition: How people allocate credit for favorable outcomes among effort, teammates, external conditions and chance.
mechanism: Self-serving explanations can narrow learning; alternative explanations depend on observable processes.
observableIndicators: A project leader credits only personal genius despite recorded team contributions.
alternativeExplanations: Different information, genuine individual influence, compensation structures.
commonMisinterpretations: All self-praise is self-delusion.

name: Practical ambition
definition: Aspirations that stretch skill and resources while remaining subject to feedback, revision and measurable outcomes.
mechanism: Goal-setting can motivate learning, but no specific effectiveness claim is established by this book alone.
observableIndicators: A founder tests assumptions and adjusts scale when evidence changes.
alternativeExplanations: Risk appetite, organizational opportunity and institutional support.
commonMisinterpretations: Any high aspiration is a sign of pathology.

name: Gender-role expectations
definition: Social rules about which behaviors, capacities or duties are considered appropriate for people labeled with particular genders.
mechanism: Norms can reward compliance and penalize departures; their content changes across periods and cultures.
observableIndicators: A father receives criticism for taking parental leave.
alternativeExplanations: Organizational rules, family circumstances, individual preference and local norms.
commonMisinterpretations: Gender-role expectations establish permanent biological capacities.

name: Gendered projection
definition: Greene/Jung’s hypothesized process of attributing idealized or disowned qualities to a partner through gendered expectations.
mechanism: Idealization is possible, but the inferred anima/animus mechanism has not been independently demonstrated here.
observableIndicators: Someone expects a partner to meet a rigid ideal and disregards stated preferences.
alternativeExplanations: Attachment patterns, norms, compatibility beliefs, situational disappointment.
commonMisinterpretations: A relationship choice reveals a person’s unconscious opposite-gender self.

name: Behavioral flexibility beyond stereotypes
definition: The freedom to select assertive, caring, analytical, collaborative or expressive behavior based on individual purpose and context.
mechanism: Exploring roles beyond social expectations may expand options; no causal effectiveness estimate is supplied by this book alone.
observableIndicators: A leader combines assertiveness and emotional attentiveness without gender labels.
alternativeExplanations: Contextual skill learning, organizational support and personal variation.
commonMisinterpretations: Flexibility requires identifying with a prescribed binary blend.

name: Deliberated purpose
definition: A chosen, revisable set of values and commitments used to organize action across time.
mechanism: Values may support prioritization without guaranteeing achievement.
observableIndicators: Repeatedly returning to a valued project after obstacles.
alternativeExplanations: Economic necessity and social reinforcement can explain persistence.
commonMisinterpretations: A single destiny must be present since childhood.

name: Goal ladder
definition: An organized sequence of feasible nearer actions linked to a broader aim.
mechanism: Intermediate goals can translate abstract purpose into actionable feedback.
observableIndicators: Creating milestones and reviewing them after new evidence.
alternativeExplanations: External planning requirements and supervision.
commonMisinterpretations: Following milestones mechanically proves personal meaning.

name: False purpose and status pursuit
definition: The possibility that prestige, group validation or stimulation substitutes for considered commitment.
mechanism: Short-lived rewards can pull attention away from reflective priorities.
observableIndicators: Switching goals mainly after external applause.
alternativeExplanations: Changing opportunities or legitimate financial requirements.
commonMisinterpretations: Money, community or pleasure is inherently a false purpose.

name: Normative group pressure
definition: Pressure to publicly act according to perceived social expectations, whether or not private belief changes.
mechanism: Potential rejection or sanctions may influence what members say.
observableIndicators: Agreeing publicly after a powerful peer endorses a proposal.
alternativeExplanations: Independent agreement, incomplete information or direct coercion.
commonMisinterpretations: Public compliance proves sincere belief.

name: Group social personality
definition: A context-dependent pattern of speech, feeling or conduct shaped by participation in a group.
mechanism: Shared cues, norms and identity can coordinate behavior.
observableIndicators: Adopting a team’s ritual or vocabulary.
alternativeExplanations: Learning useful norms or acting for strategic safety.
commonMisinterpretations: Every group member experiences the same motive.

name: Reality-oriented team
definition: A normative group design ideal emphasizing accurate information, dissent and cooperative task focus.
mechanism: Clear correction channels and mutual accountability may improve the quality of decisions.
observableIndicators: Inviting contrary evidence before a joint commitment.
alternativeExplanations: Formal governance, resource availability, or pre-existing trust.
commonMisinterpretations: A cooperative team must always reach unanimity.

name: Perceived legitimacy
definition: The extent to which people regard an exercise of authority as justified rather than simply compulsory.
mechanism: Credibility can develop through fairness, capability and predictable rule application.
observableIndicators: Leaders explain shared criteria for difficult decisions.
alternativeExplanations: Formal office, sanctions or pragmatic need may also produce compliance.
commonMisinterpretations: Popularity proves moral rightness.

name: Leadership ambivalence
definition: The coexistence of preferences for reliable direction and personal autonomy within follower–leader relationships.
mechanism: Expectations can change following successes, setbacks or perceived disrespect.
observableIndicators: A team requests guidance yet challenges an imposed rule.
alternativeExplanations: Changed information, competing interests or legitimately bad leadership.
commonMisinterpretations: Criticism is evidence of inherently fickle character.

name: Accountable authority
definition: Coordination through articulated goals, competent action, feedback and answerability rather than fear alone.
mechanism: Transparent decisions and correction processes can support reasoned trust.
observableIndicators: A project director revises plans after candid review.
alternativeExplanations: Institutional governance and group resources also shape outcomes.
commonMisinterpretations: Leaders must guarantee every outcome or demand obedience.

name: Ethical assertiveness
definition: Directly communicating needs or defending legitimate interests while respecting others’ agency and safety.
mechanism: Clear boundaries and consistent noncoercive action allow disagreement without threats.
observableIndicators: A person states a decision and supplies verifiable reasons.
alternativeExplanations: Fear or urgency may prompt strong but appropriate defensive conduct.
commonMisinterpretations: A firm refusal by itself proves hostility.

name: Instrumental intimidation
definition: Use of pressure, fear, or asymmetric power to restrict another party’s practical choices.
mechanism: Coercive pressure may make refusal or careful comparison harder; the means and context matter.
observableIndicators: Abruptly imposed deadlines and threats with consequences are documented.
alternativeExplanations: There may be genuinely binding deadlines, contractual obligations or external pressures.
commonMisinterpretations: Every urgent negotiation is intentionally manipulative.

name: Indirect conflict expression
definition: Conduct that may express disagreement or resentment without direct acknowledgement, requiring careful contextual interpretation.
mechanism: Ambiguous delays, avoidance or obstruction may be strategies but have multiple competing explanations.
observableIndicators: Recurring mismatch between stated agreements and observable actions.
alternativeExplanations: Overwork, disability, ambiguity, lack of resources or poor coordination.
commonMisinterpretations: An isolated late message is proof of passive aggression.

name: Age-period-cohort distinction
definition: Analytic separation between effects of life stage, historical events shared across ages and circumstances associated with birth cohort.
mechanism: Comparable observations across cohorts, periods and ages are needed to distinguish explanations.
observableIndicators: A study explicitly differentiates age, period and cohort rather than assuming one.
alternativeExplanations: Local institutions and individual circumstances can be more predictive.
commonMisinterpretations: A birth-year label explains a person’s beliefs.

name: Historical-period sensitivity
definition: Attention to changing institutions, technologies, conflicts and cultural practices rather than fixed demographic stereotypes.
mechanism: A changing situation can alter available goals and coordination possibilities.
observableIndicators: An organization revises policy after documented changes in access or law.
alternativeExplanations: Change may be driven by institutions or resources, not a psychological generation.
commonMisinterpretations: Being modern guarantees prescience.

name: Cohort narrative selection
definition: Retrospective storytelling that selects a few memorable actors or styles as representative of a diverse generation.
mechanism: Survivorship and hindsight can exaggerate a supposedly universal style.
observableIndicators: A history spotlights famous winners while omitting dissenters.
alternativeExplanations: Some cohorts do have shared measurable exposures, but variance remains important.
commonMisinterpretations: A famous exemplar speaks for everyone born near the same time.

name: Mortality awareness
definition: Reflective recognition of the finite and uncertain duration of individual life, distinct from any one emotional response.
mechanism: Time-horizon reflection can sometimes alter priorities but emotional outcomes vary.
observableIndicators: A person voluntarily reorders commitments after reflecting on finitude.
alternativeExplanations: Changing priorities may instead follow medical, economic or relational events.
commonMisinterpretations: Fear or reluctance to discuss death demonstrates weak character.

name: Existential meaning-making
definition: Constructing or revising personal meaning in response to limits, adversity and uncertainty.
mechanism: Beliefs, relationships and practical commitments may help organize an experience.
observableIndicators: An individual describes varied sources of value after adversity.
alternativeExplanations: Meaning and acceptance can coexist with distress and grief.
commonMisinterpretations: People have a duty to interpret suffering as beneficial.

name: Shared finitude and compassion
definition: Ethical recognition that vulnerability and mortality are common human conditions, without assuming uniform experiences.
mechanism: Awareness of vulnerability can motivate respect, mutual care and perspective taking.
observableIndicators: A community supports people with different needs during illness or loss.
alternativeExplanations: Fear and insecurity may also prompt withdrawal; the direction is not guaranteed.
commonMisinterpretations: Mortality inevitably makes every person kinder.
